name: Kaan Aksit
project_text:
"Title: Physically Informed Artificial Intelligence for Immersive Displays

Work Summary:
In the rapidly evolving world of immersive displays, there's a growing need to merge cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) techniques with physical principles to create more realistic and engaging experiences. This project offers an exciting opportunity for students in UCL's Master's program in Scientific and Data Intensive Computing to delve into the intersection of AI, physics, and display technology. By leveraging high-performance computing, optimization algorithms, and machine learning techniques, you will develop innovative solutions that push the boundaries of immersive displays. You'll explore how physical principles can inform and enhance AI models for tasks such as realistic rendering, haptic feedback, or motion tracking in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR). Through this project, you will gain hands-on experience in designing and implementing physically informed AI algorithms that drive the future of immersive displays. You'll have the chance to work with state-of-the-art hardware and software tools while collaborating with a dynamic team of researchers and industry professionals. By joining this project, you will not only contribute to groundbreaking research but also develop valuable skills in AI, high-performance computing, optimization, and data analysis that are highly sought after by both academia and industry. Don't miss out on the opportunity to make a lasting impact in the field of immersive displays—apply now for "Physically Informed Artificial Intelligence for Immersive Displays"! For more please consider visiting https://kaanaksit.com and https://complightlab.com."

name: Timo Betcke
project_text:
"Title: GPU computing in Rust

Work Summary:
Rust is a relatively new systems programming language that has growing popularity in Scientific Computing. Where Rust is still lacking though is good support for GPU acceleration. In this project we want to investigate available GPU computing toolkits for Rust, setup benchmark experiments and investigate how to evolve the Rust GPU computing ecosystem. If you are interested, please apply by the end of October at the latest by sending me your CV and a brief outline of previous programming experience. Please note that I expect the successful applicant to dedicate substantial time to the project throughout the whole academic year."

name: Nikos Nikolaou
project_text:
"Title: Uncertainty estimation & interpretability of machine learning models for medical imaging

Prerequisites:
The student must have good knowledge of Python and experience with machine learning – ideally related to medical applications and/or imaging.

Work Summary:
The project will focus on training and evaluating machine learning models in the context of a medical imaging task (to be decided with the interested student). The primary objective will be to investigate the models' predictions using model evaluation and model interpretability methods to identify under what conditions the model predictions fail, to better understand biases in the models and/or the data and perhaps to uncover interesting features in the image that can be of clinical interest. We will mainly focus on assessing and improving the models' uncertainty quantification (how certain a model is about its predictions) and what effect doing so will have on interpretability. Depending on the student's interests, the project will lean more on the uncertainty quantification or the interpretability aspect.

Scientific aims:
The project will investigate machine learning models trained in a medical imaging task of interest to the student. The focus of the project will be on investigating the effect improving the model's uncertainty estimation will have on explaining the predictions of the models. Identifying what patterns the models associate with what predictions—especially in situations where such predictions are wrong—will help us understand the extent to which the models are trustworthy or the conditions in which the models fail. This in turn can help improve their performance, identify bias in training data and improve the adoption of automated medical imaging models in this setting. Improving the quality of a model's uncertainty quantification can directly help users balance costs and benefits of actions related to the model's prediction (e.g. of possible treatments). It can also potentially indirectly improve the model's interpretability, by capturing more relevant underlying features and their relationship with the target.

Overview:
The student will learn to handle real world imaging data with all its complications (need to align images, need for data augmentation and/or imputation, handling multiple data types and class imbalance). They will also learn to train state of the art machine learning models for medical imaging (CNNs or ViTs) using rigorous methodology to fine-tune and evaluate them. If time permits they will explore transfer learning or ensemble learning methods to further improve performance. Most importantly, they will learn about (1) model interpretability methods for deep neural networks and how to integrate them in their investigation to understand, improve and extract relevant domain knowledge from the models and (2) how to measure and improve the quality of uncertainty quantification of a model. Depending on the student's interests, the project will lean more on the uncertainty quantification or the interpretability aspect.

-----
Title: Beyond backpropagation: exploring alternative ways of training deep learning models

Prerequisites:
The student must have a strong mathematical and algorithmic background, good knowledge of Python and experience with deep learning frameworks (Pytorch, Tensorflow, Keras).

Work Summary:
Backpropagation has been the cornerstone of deep learning optimization for decades. However, it suffers from biological implausibility, high memory usage, and limitations in parallelism. This project proposes to explore alternative training paradigms that eliminate the need for global gradient propagation—namely, local learning rules, Hebbian updates, feedback alignment, target propagation, and emerging frameworks such as NoProp, which eliminates both forward and backward passes. Our goal is to implement and benchmark these methods on tasks like image classification and sequence modeling using standard architectures. We will evaluate them in terms of performance, scalability, computational cost, and generalization ability. Additionally, we aim to investigate how these alternative training methods intersect with network sparsity and pruning strategies inspired by the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH). Ultimately, this research could advance understanding of more efficient, scalable, and biologically inspired learning mechanisms and offer new perspectives on model training dynamics and network initialization.

Key References:

Bengio, Y., Lee, D. H., Bornschein, J., & Lin, Z. (2017). Towards Biologically Plausible Deep Learning. arXiv:1502.04156
Nøkland, A. (2016). Direct Feedback Alignment Provides Learning in Deep Neural Networks. arXiv:1609.01596
Hebbian Updates
Gerstner, W., Kempter, R., van Hemmen, J. L., & Wagner, H. (1996). A neuronal learning rule for sub-millisecond temporal coding. Nature
Pehlevan, C., & Chklovskii, D. B. (2019). Optimization theory of Hebbian/anti-Hebbian networks for PCA and whitening. NeurIPS
Feedback Alignment
Lillicrap, T. P., Cownden, D., Tweed, D. B., & Akerman, C. J. (2016). Random synaptic feedback weights support error backpropagation for deep learning. Nature Communications
Murray, J. M. (2019). Local online learning in recurrent networks with random feedback. eLife
Target Propagation
Lee, D. H., Zhang, S., Fischer, A., & Bengio, Y. (2015). Difference Target Propagation. ECML PKDD
Bartunov, S., Santoro, A., Richards, B. A., Marris, L., Hinton, G., & Lillicrap, T. (2018). Assessing the Scalability of Biologically-Motivated Deep Learning Algorithms. NeurIPS
NoProp Approach

Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH)

project_text:
Title: Large-scale molecular graphics of convex-body fluid

Supervisor 1 email address: g.germano@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: TBA

Supervisor 2 email address: TBA

Work Summary:
1. Update all the library calls and the makefile so that QMGA compiles on Linux.
2. Move the distribution to GitHub.
3. Modify the source code to exploit the most recent developments of OpenGL in order to improve the
program’s performance e.g. along the lines described in Section 4 of the paper (occlusion queries, backface
culling, the use of vertex buffer objects, etc.).
4. Port the final result to macOS and Windows.
5. Additionally or alternatively to using OpenGL, rewrite the program basing it on WebGL and thus JavaScript
so that it works always and everywhere, and is as fast as with C++ without worrying any more about builds,
libraries, compilers and compatibility. This is based on the advice of Professor Tobias Ritschel, UCL, who is the
module leader of COMP0027 Computer Graphics and has been using WebGL for all his teaching since 2015;
see http://vecg.cs.ucl.ac.uk/ . This evolution would be released with the new name WebMGA.
Obviously the most interesting parts are 3 and 5, but 1, 2 and 4 would be useful too along the way.

Scientific aims:
Improve the performance of QMGA.

Overview:
==== WebMGA: Large-scale molecular graphics of convex-body fluids ====
QMGA is a molecular graphics program written in C++ and based on the OpenGL, QT and Glut libraries. It is
available open source for Linux on http://qmga.sourceforge.net , where you can also find the PDF of a
paper (https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/ct700192z) which describes it and has been published in the Journal of
Chemical Theory and Computation (impact factor = 5.011). In October 2020, this paper has been cited 62
times on Google Scholar, 48 times on Web of Science and 48 times on Scopus.
In the interactive, rendered representation of large ensembles of convex bodies performance is crucial
because typical sizes arising in state-of-the-art coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of e.g. liquid
crystals on massively parallel computers increase from year to year, from a few thousands 20 years ago to 100
000 when the program was first published and millions nowadays. In its niche, this program is still without
rivals for features, interactivity and speed. Although it has been open source since 2008, unfortunately the
hope has not been fulfilled that the development of the code is picked up by a community; instead, users write
me asking for help because it does not compile any more straight away. Therefore developments (after some
unavoidable maintenance) are proposed as this MSc project:
1. Update all the library calls and the makefile so that QMGA compiles on Linux.
2. Move the distribution to GitHub.
3. Modify the source code to exploit the most recent developments of OpenGL in order to improve the
program’s performance e.g. along the lines described in Section 4 of the paper (occlusion queries, backface
culling, the use of vertex buffer objects, etc.).
4. Port the final result to macOS and Windows.
5. Additionally or alternatively to using OpenGL, rewrite the program basing it on WebGL and thus JavaScript
so that it works always and everywhere, and is as fast as with C++ without worrying any more about builds,
libraries, compilers and compatibility. This is based on the advice of Professor Tobias Ritschel, UCL, who is the
module leader of COMP0027 Computer Graphics and has been using WebGL for all his teaching since 2015;
see http://vecg.cs.ucl.ac.uk/ . This evolution would be released with the new name WebMGA.
Obviously the most interesting parts are 3 and 5, but 1, 2 and 4 would be useful too along the way.

name: Mose Giordano
project_text:
Title: Implementation of Lomb-Scargle algorithm in Julia

Supervisor 1 email address: m.giordano@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: David Perez-Suarez

Supervisor 2 email address: d.perez-suarez@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
The Lomb-Scargle periodogram is a technique commonly used in Astronomy to detect the period of a periodic,
possibly unevenly sampled, signal (e.g. light curves of variable stars). Dr Giordano is the author
of https://github.com/JuliaAstro/LombScargle.jl, an open-source package which collects some
implementations of the Lomb-Scargle periodogram in Julia, a high-level programming language for scientific
computing. There is another algorithm, based on the non-equispaced fast Fourier transform, which is
supposed to deliver better performance than the other algorithms implemented in LombScargle.jl. The goal of
this project is to write a high-performance implementation of this algorithm in Julia, contributing to the
LombScargle.jl package, and compare its performance with the other algorithms. An overview of the work to
do is available at https://github.com/JuliaAstro/LombScargle.jl/issues/8.

name: Peter Bentley
project_text:
Title: Deep Morphogenesis: Distributed Generative Design using Machine Learning

Supervisor 1 email address: p.bentley@cs.ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Soo Ling LIM

Supervisor 2 email address: s.lim@cs.ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Some experience of machine learning and/or evolutionary computation useful. Python programming essential.

Work Summary:
The work will involve becoming familiar with the existing state of the art, and then building from it with the aim
of learning more about how ML can enhance generative design and our ability to use computers to generate
novel complex forms that perform a specific function. At least one new model that can generate a complex
form will be attempted.
• Please send a CV

Scientific aims:
In this project the aim is to achieve a similar kind of generative design. Methods such as generative adversarial
networks or variational autoencoders will enable the generation of a representation with the right properties for
development: the right amount of expressiveness, useful bias, evolvability to enable effective search,
adaptability and efficiency. This representation combined with methods such as cellular automata or multi
agent system will enable the generation of different forms, akin to [1] and [2]. Techniques such as genetic
algorithms or novelty search will enable the exploration of different forms using this representation, e.g. the
methods in [3]. The result would be a distributed generative design process that generates a complex desired
form efficiently in the same way that nature does it - using combining learned information with iterative growth
and interaction from an environment such that it meets new constraints, resulting in a shape massively more
complex than the 'instructions' needed to define it. It would also be a novel combination of AI techniques that
expand the capabilities of all.
[1] Mordvintsev, et al., "Growing Neural Cellular Automata", Distill, 2020. https://distill.pub/2020/growing-ca/
[2] Lomas, A. “Morphogenetic Forms”. Artworks and videos. https://andylomas.com/videos.html
[3] Kumar, S. and Bentley, P. J. (Contributing Eds.) (2003) On Growth, Form and Computers. Academic Press,
London.

Overview:
Generative design is big business today. Automatically creating 3D geometries such that form fits function is
many orders of magnitude more complex than working with 2D images. Get it right and you can auto generate
building designs, aerodynamic forms, engine components – vital applications for companies such as Autodesk
and its customers.
Current approaches used in industry rely on genetic algorithms to optimize forms. More recent work uses deep
learning to generate forms based on large datasets of existing designs. These approaches show useful results
but they are limited in complexity and limited by data – GAs can find novelty but they struggle to find complex
forms, and deep learning cannot innovate: its solutions are always variants of past designs and it doesn’t adapt

them to new environments. We need a method that combines ideas from both.
Nature teaches us some amazing lessons when it comes to intelligence and has inspired many fields of AI from
deep learning to evolutionary computation. But an often-overlooked example of intelligence is development -
the process of embryogenesis that builds all complex forms of life (including the brain) through interactions
between genes, cells and environments. Development combines evolution with gene regulatory networks and
runs a genetic program in parallel across all our cells. It works because the representation (our DNA) contains
lessons learned from unthinkable numbers of challenges faced. It also works because development is not a
blueprint, but a way of building morphology in combination with an environment – change the environment and
the form changes to match.

-----
Title: Evolving Latent Variables

Supervisor 1 email address: p.bentley@cs.ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: TBA

Supervisor 2 email address: TBA

Work Summary:
Optimization and exploration only works when given an appropriate representation. It is the (genetic)
representation that defines the searchspace, and we can map to a new representation (phenotype) in order to
evaluate that quality of the solution. But designing a good representation that defines a smooth, searchable
space is something of an art form, especially when the problem may naturally be massively multivariate,
discontinuous, noisy, multiobjective, or constrained. In this project the aim is to use generative ML such as
GANs or autoencoders such as VAEs to learn the representation from examples of existing solutions to the
problem (or similar problems). We then use an optimizer such as a genetic algorithm to search in the latent
space, and use the learned neural model to map from the evolved latent variables to the phenotype so that we
can evaluate the solutions. This idea is becoming popular and looks to be the future of optimization. But how
best to learn latent spaces? GANs enable more precise representations, and some level of latent variable
disentanglement can be achieved; VAEs are more fuzzy but have encoders and decoders enabling us to search
in latent spaces and original spaces simultaneously and translate between them. How do they compare? Or
would other generative approaches work better? We have shown this works for constrained optimization but
will it work for difficult real world problems? Or for multiobjective optimization? For reading material on this
topic, check out papers such as these:
https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Tf8winBIYUsC&hl=en
https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=GGyARB8AAAAJ&hl=en&oi=sra
https://doi.org/10.1145/3520304.3533993
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-14714-2_26

name: Edina Rosta
project_text:
Title: Design and Development of Autoencoders to Identify Latent Space for Protein Dynamics

Supervisor 1 email address: e.rosta@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Sam Martino

Supervisor 2 email address: sam.martino.20@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Students with background on Data Science, Machine Learning, Biophysics or Computational Chemistry are
encouraged to apply, but it is not required. Knowledge of Python programming language is also recommended,
as well as experience in scripting and Linux/bash systems. MATLAB is also a plus, but not needed. TensorFlow
and Scikit-Learn knowledge is also valued.

Work Summary:
· Learning to perform and/or visualise MD simulation data on biomolecular systems.
· Learning to use Python for data analysis and parse MD trajectories.
· Applying ML architectures e.g., autoencoders for unsupervised classification of MD data.
· Analysis of trained ML models to understand key collective variables in the latent space.
· Use of the ML models for further sampling.
• Students are expected to send their CV along with a bit of information on their background and what experience
they previously had.

Scientific aims:
· Generate and/or parse molecular dynamics trajectories for ML input
· Apply and train ML architectures to perform unsupervised learning for conformational changes taking place in
the system
· Analyse trained ML models to extract key dynamical features

Overview:
Recent AI-based structure prediction of biological systems has shown extraordinary successes, e.g., by
Google’s AlphaFold. Understanding protein conformational sampling nevertheless is still one of the two main
development areas for large scale atomistic biomolecular simulations besides force field development. To
extract relevant collective variables that describe the key features of the protein dynamics is a challenging
task, due to the high dimensionality data driven by complex interactions. Here we will explore recent machine
learning (ML) methods to develop tools that characterise the time evolution of protein dynamics and help
predict structural changes leading to the protein function.

-----
Title: Combining Machine Learning and Molecular Dynamics Simulations for the Selection of Relevant Collective Variables

Supervisor 1 email address: e.rosta@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Pedro Buigues

Supervisor 2 email address: pedro.jorro.20@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Students with background on Machine Learning, Biophysical systems or Computational Chemistry is useful but
not required. Experience with Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations is helpful but not required. Knowledge of
Python programming language is also recommended, as well as experience in scripting and Linux/bash
systems. TensorFlow and Scikit-Learn knowledge is also valued.

Work Summary:
· Understanding protein unbinding processes, including elements of structural biology.
· Learn to perform MD simulations and use analysis tools to gather relevant data and create datasets
(Pymol/VMD).
· Apply data visualization to find relevant reaction coordinates for biological systems.

· Create/Improve code to automate the finding of relevant variables in protein unbinding trajectories.
· Getting familiar with Machine Learning (ML) models such as Neural Networks (MLP, RNN, LSTM
architectures) and Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (Scikit-Learn and TensorFlow).
· Evaluations and limitations of the models and their applicability.
• Students are expected to send their CV along with a bit of information on their background and what experience
they previously had.

Scientific aims:
· Parse through MD data (cartesian coordinates of millions of atoms) for further analysis.
· Develop and apply ML models to learn protein unbinding classification.
· Explore and understand the MLTSA results at the high-dimensional space.
· Implement other methodologies for relevant feature identification.

Overview:
Ligand unbinding is a vital part of drug design, Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations allow us to witness these
events at high resolution, analyse the data and find relevant information that will allow us to tweak small
molecules to alter their pharmacokinetic properties. This procedure results in large amounts of data to analyse,
which requires automated methods. This project focuses on applying and developing a Machine Learning
Transition State Analysis (MLTSA) method for MD simulations to identify the relevant features in large datasets
of the ligand unbinding events. Extensive analysis of these features can be used to better sample these
processes, to understand in detail the protein involvement, and to suggest future design for optimizing
molecules with long residence times.

-----
Title: Markov models with reinforcement learning for enhanced sampling simulations

Supervisor 1 email address: e.rosta@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Balint Dudas

Supervisor 2 email address: b.dudas@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Essential: Python; basic ML (PyTorch/TF or scikit-learn); numerics; comfort with Linux/CLI.
Helpful: Any of OpenMM/MD basics or RL (PPO/SAC) concepts.
Training and starter code will be provided; the project can be steered more toward RL/ML, simulation, or
statistical validation depending on the student.

Work Summary:
The student will start from existing PPO/SAC code integrating Gaussian bias potentials with Langevin
dynamics (OpenMM), where the agent learns to accelerate barrier crossings. We will (i) standardise
environments (analytical → Langevin → simple MD), (ii) refine agent interfaces (continuous actions,
entropy/clip tuning), (iii) add baselines (MFPT-driven MD) for apples-to-apples comparisons. Deliverables
include a reproducible pipeline (envs, agents, baselines, metrics), comparative plots, and a short manuscript-
style report.

Scientific aims:
Robust RL biasing on physical simulators
Stabilise PPO/SAC agents for Langevin/MD environments with continuous actions (bias
centre/width/height), curriculum difficulty, and safe-exploration constraints to prevent unphysical forces
and have a more efficient performance.
Generalise state and reward representations
Move beyond handcrafted 1D states to richer encodings (local energy/forces, short trajectory snippets,
MSM-derived slow coordinates), and compare goal-based (distance/progress) vs kinetics-aware
(MFPT/success-bonus) rewards.
Prototype scaling beyond 1D
Demonstrate transfer to a 2D model surface (e.g., double-well + orthogonal coordinate) or a minimal
biomolecular CV pair, testing multi-Gaussian or adaptive bias fields.
Enhanced simulation protocol for a biomolecular example, including protein dynamics.

Benchmark against established enhanced sampling
Head-to-head comparisons with other methods; report MFPT, barrier-crossing rate, state coverage, and
estimator variance.
Pathway validation
Validate the likelihood of obtaining an observed pathway vs unbiased mechanism.

Overview:
This project advances a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework for autonomous bias placement to
accelerate rare events in molecular simulations. Building on your prior integration of PPO/SAC/A2C with
Langevin dynamics and Markov State Models (MSMs)—where the agent optimised Gaussian bias
parameters and improved sampling efficiency on 1D analytical and Langevin benchmarks—this extension will (i)
make the method more efficient, (ii) scale it beyond toy models, and (iii) establish baselines for physically
meaningful observables, such as mechanistic pathways.

-----
Title: Biasing sampling on networks

Supervisor 1 email address: e.rosta@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Fahim Faizi

Supervisor 2 email address: f.faizi.14@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Good working knowledge of Matlab is required. Interest and knowledge about ML methods, Python
programming is also desirable.

Work Summary:
We will explore algorithms to bias the sampling of kinetic networks. We will use stochastic block model and
other, real data-derived networks as a starting point, and run dynamical trajectories on the network nodes
using a kinetic Monte Carlo algorithm.
We will develop measures to assess the efficiency of sampling, which will serve to identify a suitable loss
function. We will also apply bias on the network, aiming to develop a history-dependent sampling where the
bias is optimally applied. We will use ML-based optimization to determine the required bias.

Scientific aims:
Sampling problems are notoriously difficult, especially for high-dimensional systems. Here we will aim to
develop ML-assisted sampling algorithms that improve sampling by applying bias in high-dimensional

problems such as for complex networks.

-----
Title: Machine Learning–Driven Functional Classification of NTP-Processing Enzymes

Supervisor 1 email address: e.rosta@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Balint Dudas

Supervisor 2 email address: b.dudas@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Basic Python programming: some familiarity with data handling using libraries such as pandas, numpy,
and matplotlib.
Introductory machine learning knowledge: understanding of model training, validation, and
performance evaluation (e.g., using scikit-learn or PyTorch).
General understanding of protein structure and enzyme function (e.g., active sites, cofactors,
catalytic residues) is useful.
Helpful but not essential:
Experience with bioinformatics tools or databases (UniProt, PDB, InterPro, or AlphaFold/Protenix).
Familiarity with sequence embeddings or deep learning models for proteins (e.g., ESM, ProtBERT).
Interest in structural enzymology or computational biochemistry, particularly mechanisms of
ATP/GTP hydrolysis.
Training provided:
All domain-specific training (e.g., enzyme annotation systems, use of Protenix and DALI, feature extraction
pipelines, and model interpretation tools) will be provided during the project. The student will develop practical
skills in data curation, feature engineering, and machine learning applied to biological problems.

Work Summary:
This project will investigate how information encoded in protein sequences determines three-dimensional
structure and ultimately biochemical function. The student will use a combination of bioinformatics and
machine learning approaches to identify sequence and structural patterns that distinguish proteins with
different catalytic or binding activities. Using curated datasets from UniProt, PDB, and InterPro, the project
will integrate modern protein language models and structural prediction tools (e.g., AlphaFold or Protenix)
to derive descriptors that capture functionally relevant features such as active-site geometry, metal-ion
coordination, or ligand-binding motifs.
Machine learning models will then be trained to predict the functional class or Enzyme Commission (EC)
number of proteins from these features, and results will be benchmarked against established bioinformatics
annotation pipelines. Through this work, the student will gain experience in computational protein science,
including data curation, feature engineering, and model development, while contributing to the broader
understanding of how sequence diversity shapes protein function across enzyme families.

Scientific aims:
Uncover sequence–structure–function relationships in proteins
Identify how variations in amino acid sequence give rise to distinct structural motifs, active-site
geometries, and catalytic functions across enzyme families.
Develop computational models for protein function prediction
Build and evaluate machine learning models that integrate sequence embeddings and structural features
to classify proteins by functional category (e.g., EC number or catalytic mechanism).
Characterise structural determinants of enzymatic specificity
Determine which sequence or structural features—such as cofactor-binding motifs, metal coordination
sites, or residue conservation patterns—most strongly influence functional outcomes.

Benchmark and validate predictive approaches
Compare the performance of data-driven models against existing bioinformatics annotation tools (e.g.,
SUPFAM, InterPro, DALI) and assess their ability to predict or refine enzyme function assignments.
Enable functional annotation of uncharacterised proteins
Apply the trained models to unannotated or poorly characterised protein sequences to propose testable
hypotheses about their molecular roles, supporting future experimental validation.

Overview:
Understanding how protein sequence determines structure and function is a central challenge in molecular
biology. Despite the success of structural prediction tools such as AlphaFold, linking these predicted
structures to specific biochemical functions remains a major unsolved problem. This project aims to bridge
that gap by developing computational and machine learning approaches that connect sequence information to
protein function across diverse enzyme families.
The student will assemble and analyse large datasets of protein sequences and structures from resources
such as UniProt, PDB, and InterPro, extracting features that describe active-site geometry, residue
conservation, and cofactor-binding motifs. These data will be used to train machine learning models capable
of predicting functional classes (e.g., Enzyme Commission numbers) directly from sequence and structure-
derived descriptors.
By integrating methods from bioinformatics, data science, and computational biochemistry, the project will
provide new insights into the determinants of enzyme specificity and catalysis. The broader goal is to advance
automated protein annotation and improve our ability to predict function for the growing number of
uncharacterised proteins emerging from large-scale sequencing efforts.

-----
Title: Causal Inference and Mechanistic Discovery in Complex Time-Series Data

Supervisor 1 email address: e.rosta@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Balint Dudas

Supervisor 2 email address: b.dudas@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Essential skills:
Basic proficiency in Python programming and data handling (numpy, pandas, matplotlib).

Familiarity with statistics and time-series concepts (e.g., correlation, regression, or basic signal
analysis).
Interest in the principles of causality, mechanistic modeling, or complex system dynamics.
Desirable (but not essential):
Experience with machine learning or graph-based models (scikit-learn, networkx, or pytorch).
Exposure to simulation data analysis (e.g., molecular dynamics, agent-based models, or physical
simulations).
Knowledge of basic probability theory or information theory concepts (entropy, mutual information).
Training provided:
Students will receive hands-on training in causal inference algorithms, model evaluation, and scientific data
visualization. The project can be tailored to emphasize data science, physics, or biomolecular applications
depending on the student’s background and interests.

Work Summary:
This project will apply causal inference techniques to identify directional relationships within complex
biological and physical systems. While traditional data analysis methods reveal correlations between variables,
they cannot determine which processes drive others. The student will explore how causal discovery
algorithms—such as PC, PCMCI, VAR-LiNGAM, and Transfer Entropy—can be used to extract cause–effect
networks from diverse time-series data, including analytical models, publicly available datasets, and
molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.
The project will begin with controlled synthetic datasets to benchmark and validate different causal algorithms,
before extending the analysis to more complex biological and physical systems. By comparing methods and
quantifying their robustness, the student will help establish best practices for applying causal inference to
time-dependent scientific data.
Through this work, the student will gain experience in time-series analysis, causal discovery, and
computational modeling, developing transferable skills that bridge data science, physics, and molecular
biology. The project will contribute to a growing effort to move beyond correlation-based approaches and
toward mechanistic understanding of dynamic systems.

Scientific aims:
Develop and benchmark causal discovery methods for molecular systems
Evaluate and compare existing causal inference algorithms (e.g., PC, PCMCI, VAR-LiNGAM, Transfer
Entropy) using synthetic and molecular dynamics (MD) datasets to identify robust approaches for
detecting directional dependencies in biomolecular trajectories.
Quantify causal relationships between structural and dynamical variables
Apply causal inference to MD simulations to determine which molecular coordinates (residues, distances,
dihedral angles, solvent interactions) act as causal drivers of conformational transitions, binding events,
or allosteric communication.
Validate causal insights against physical and biochemical knowledge
Test the inferred causal networks against known mechanistic models of protein motion or ligand binding
to assess their physical plausibility and interpretability.
Establish a general workflow for causal analysis of biomolecular simulations
Integrate trajectory preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, causal discovery, and visualization into a
reproducible computational pipeline applicable across protein and nucleic acid systems.

Explore applications to mechanistic and drug discovery problems
Demonstrate how causal inference can reveal functionally relevant pathways, identify key residues or
water-mediated couplings, and generate hypotheses for experimental testing or structure-based design.

Overview:
Traditional molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provide rich time-resolved data on biomolecular motions but
often rely on correlation-based analyses, which cannot reveal the true direction of molecular influence. This
project applies causal discovery methods to uncover the underlying cause–effect relationships governing
protein–ligand interactions and conformational changes.
Using timeseries from databases and MD simulations, the project will benchmark several causal inference
algorithms (e.g., PC, PCMCI, Transfer Entropy, and VAR-LiNGAM) to determine their performance on
synthetic and real molecular datasets. The best-performing approach will then be applied to identify causal
pathways linking key residues and solvent molecules during ligand binding and unbinding events.
By integrating computational biophysics with causal inference and time-series analysis, the project aims
to move beyond correlations to reveal the mechanistic drivers of conformational transitions in proteins. The
broader goal is to establish general frameworks for applying causal discovery to biomolecular simulations,
ultimately providing insights relevant to drug design, allosteric regulation, and molecular mechanism
elucidation.

Scientific aims:
This project will investigate if some these techniques can be adapted to the lung, which has several challenges
including air content and heterogeneous uptake.

Overview:
Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging is a common technique to image functional processes. By
injecting a radiotracer, metabolic processes related to that molecule can be measured in vivo. There is
increasing interest in imaging the diseased lung, with projects at UCL/H including post-COVID-19 scanning
with multiple radiotracers.
However, due to the physics processes involved in doing the PET measurement as well limitations on
(radioactive) dose to the patient, spatial resolution of PET is limited to about 5mm in the thorax. For certain
radionuclides, positron range degrades the resolution even more, especially in the lung due to its low density.
This reduced spatial resolution impacts quantification and is called the “partial volume effect” (PVE).
Several techniques have been developed to correct for PVE, ranging from model-based, deconvolution to
machine learning using convolutional neural networks [1]. However, these techniques have mostly been
developed for, and evaluated in, brain application.
This project will be working within a research framework on standardisation of lung imaging with PET in a
collaboration between the Institute of Nuclear Medicine at UCL/UCLH and the UK National Physical Laboratory.
[1] Erlandsson, Kjell, Irène Buvat, P. Hendrik Pretorius, Benjamin A. Thomas, and Brian F. Hutton. ‘A Review of
Partial Volume Correction Techniques for Emission Tomography and Their Applications in Neurology,
Cardiology and Oncology’. Physics in Medicine and Biology 57, no. 21 (November 2012): R119–59.
https://doi.org/10.1088/0031-9155/57/21/r119 .

Title: Using Deep Learning to estimate average PET sensitivity to correct for motion in PET

Supervisor 1 email address: k.thielemans@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Sam Porter

Supervisor 2 email address: sam.porter.18@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Programming experience essential, ideally Python or MATLAB. Basic knowledge of CNN architectures for
imaging and training desired but not required. Interest of making meaningful contributions to research.

Work Summary:
In Positron Emission Tomography (PET) a radiotracer is injected and its distribution is measured, allowing to
investigate metabolic processes related to that molecule in vivo. In the thorax, patient motion is unavoidable in
standard clinical scans due to the scan duration (~2 minutes). Several methods have been developed to
correct the motion by splitting data in different motion states and taking motion into account during
reconstruction. However, as the measured photons are attenuated, the effective sensitivity varies locally as
well as with motion. This needs to be taken into account, but the relevant calculation is often the most
computationally expensive part.
The aim of this project is to investigate the use of CNNs to compute how the effective sensitivity changes with
motion. This is a novel approach and could lead to publication.

Title: Using machine learning techniques to denoise SPECT images for quantitative accuracy

Supervisor 1 email address: k.thielemans@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Cate Gascoigne

Supervisor 2 email address: cate.cascoigne.23@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Programming experience and a basic understanding of machine learning is essential. An interest in medical
imaging and quantitative analysis is desirable.

Overview:
Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) is a three-dimensional medical imaging technique. A
radiopharmaceutical ‘tracer’ is administered to the patient and accumulates in organs or processes under
investigation. For example, radiopharmaceuticals which bind to proteins found on certain types of tumours can
be used to detect and evaluate cancer. Gamma photons emitted by the tracer can be detected outside the
body using a gamma camera. This information is converted into a three-dimensional image representing the
distribution of the tracer, allowing clinicians to infer functional information. This can help to diagnose the
patient’s condition, monitor disease progression and assess the effectiveness of any treatments.
For many years, clinical evaluation of SPECT images has been mainly qualitative, i.e. clinicians report what they
can see in the images without access to quantitative metrics. Improvements in technology and advances the
development of cancer treatments have led to increased interest in quantitative SPECT imaging. This allows
clinicians to estimate absolute quantities of tracer uptake within volumes of interest. This is useful for
assessing the extent of disease, planning treatments and comparing uptake between timepoints to evaluate
progression.
Due to limitations associated with SPECT, image quality can be poor, and quantification is inaccurate. Low
spatial resolution and low sensitivity (the proportion of gamma photons emitted which contribute to the final
image) lead to blurry and noisy images. It is difficult to distinguish structures from the background and
estimate their true size and tracer concentration. Traditionally, image quality has been understood as a
compromise between spatial resolution and sensitivity. However, machine learning (ML) introduces the
possibility of overcoming this trade-off.
This project will focus on using state-of-the-art ML techniques to denoise SPECT images and achieve
quantitative accuracy, particularly in small volumes of interest. The work will build on two recent projects which
our group has participated in. The first project compared the denoising performance of three models (a 3D U-

Net, a projection-domain single-step PDPM (Poisson diffusion-based 3D U-Net), and Swin UNETR) on
simulated and clinical data. The second project trained a 2D U-Net to denoise simulated and clinical data and
assessed quantitative accuracy in small volumes (tumours). Possible areas to expand the research include:
· Generating a large, diverse and clinically realistic training dataset, for example using Monte Carlo
simulation.
· Investigating model architectures, hyperparameters, loss functions and training strategies to overcome the
class imbalance that arises because volumes of interest are only a small proportion of the total image volume.
This project will use open-source image simulation and reconstruction software.

References:
Hutton, B. F.; Erlandsson, K.; Thielemans, K. Quantification in Emission Tomography. In Handbook of
Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging for Physicists; CRC Press, 2022; Vol. 1.
Balaji, V.; Song, T.-A.; Malekzadeh, M.; Heidari, P.; Dutta, J. Artificial Intelligence for PET and SPECT Image
Enhancement. Journal of Nuclear Medicine 2023. https://doi.org/10.2967/jnumed.122.265000.

Title: Evaluation of Energy Based Scatter Correction for PET

Supervisor 1 email address: k.thielemans@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Antonia Reeves

Supervisor 2 email address: antonia.reeves.22@ucl.ac.uk

Overview:
Summary:
In Positron Emission Tomography (PET), a radiotracer is injected into the body. As the radiotracer decays, it
emits positrons. These positrons interact with nearby electrons, resulting in a process called annihilation,
where two photons are emitted in opposite directions, approximately 180º apart. PET scanners detect these
photons to create detailed images of structures such as tumours, the heart, and the brain.
However, sometimes these photons undergo a process known as Compton scattering. As the photons travel
through the body, they may interact with tissues and other matter, causing their path to change. This
scattering distorts the spatial information, since the photons no longer travel in straight lines. As a result, both
image accuracy and quantitative reliability in PET are reduced.
The main method of scatter estimation is using Single Scatter Simulation (SSS). This uses a density image (or
attenuation map) of the body to simulate where photons will scatter. However, this only accounts for single

scatter events (photons that scatter once) and can be computationally expensive.
Recently, alternative methods have been developed that exploit the fact that Compton scatter decreases the
energy of the photons. [1,2,3] They do this by developing a Probability Density Function (PDF) to estimate the
probability of the type of interaction that is recorded given the energy of the 2 recorded photons. There have
been several methods of PDF calculation published.
This project will evaluate the impact of different PDF calculation methods on scatter estimation using our
open-source software STIR. [4] We will investigate approaches such as the Method of Moments and Maximum
Likelihood estimation for fitting PDFs to the energy distribution. Using STIR, we will also compare these scatter
estimates against current methods such as SSS and assess their effect on reconstructed image quality.
Depending on the outcomes, this may also open opportunities to develop and evaluate deep learning
approaches for energy based scatter estimation.
Prerequisites: Programming experience (python or C++ preferable), basic knowledge of PET would be
recommended.
References:
[1] J. J. Hamill, J. Cabello, S. Surti, and J. S. Karp, ‘Energy-based scatter estimation in clinical PET’, Medical
Physics, vol. 51, no. 1, pp. 54–69, 2024, doi: 10.1002/mp.16826.
[2] N. Efthimiou, J. S. Karp, and S. Surti, ‘Data-driven, Energy-based method for estimation of Scattered events
in Positron Emission Tomography’, Phys Med Biol, vol. 67, no. 9, p. 10.1088/1361-6560/ac62fc, Apr. 2022, doi:
10.1088/1361-6560/ac62fc.
[3] L. M. Popescu, R. M. Lewitt, S. Matej, and J. S. Karp, ‘PET energy-based scatter estimation and image
reconstruction with energy-dependent corrections’, Phys. Med. Biol., vol. 51, no. 11, p. 2919, May 2006, doi:
10.1088/0031-9155/51/11/016.
[4] I. Polycarpou, K. Thielemans, et al., Comparative Evaluation of Scatter Correction in 3D PET Using Different
Scatter-Level Approximations. Annals of Nuclear Medicine 2011, 25 (9), 643–649.
https://doi.org/10.1007/s12149-011-0514-y.

Scientific aims:
This project is to develop code that can be used to process and range of images (JPEG, TIF, PNG) and frames
from movies (MPEG, AVI) and apply the BOS method to them to image various chemical and physical changes
of a material. Further, the code should be able to analyse images from a plenoptic camera. It should create a

For example, recent work has used classic Schlieren to look at mixing of water and alcohol. Demonstrating

Overview:
Background Orientated Schlieren (BOS) is a method to examine changes in density in materials, classically
used to examine gas flows above hot sources or discontinuities in wind tunnels. BOS relies on computational
processing to look for minute differences between images to generate new images of any density changes.
When this is coupled with a Plenoptic (or light field, http://www.plenoptic.info/) camera (that both detects the
intensity of light and its direction) it is possible to create 3D images of the change in density. This involves
handling a large number of files and performing complicated analysis procedures.

Title: Enhancing Statistical Comparisons in YODA Using Eigen

Supervisor 1 email address: b.waugh@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Christian Gutschow

Supervisor 2 email address: c.gutschow@ucl.ac.uk

Work Summary:
YODA is a key software library used in particle physics for comparing
theoretical predictions with experimental data. At present, it supports
only a simplified version of the chi-squared (chi2) test, ignoring
correlations between data points.
This project will introduce full chi-squared support using the Eigen C++
library, while keeping it an optional dependency to maintain YODA’s
lightweight nature. You’ll also modernise YODA’s interface with the
Contur reinterpretation tool to better handle detailed uncertainty
information.
The project is well-suited for students interested in scientific
software and real-world physics applications. You’ll contribute to a
widely used open-source codebase and gain practical experience in
applied statistics and high-performance C++ development.

Title: Applying machine learning techniques to test new theories in particle physics

Supervisor 1 email address: b.waugh@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Jon Butterworth

Supervisor 2 email address: j.butterworth@ucl.ac.uk

Work Summary:
A major area of research in particle physics is testing new BSM (Beyond
the Standard Model) theories by comparing their predictions with known
experimental results. This is a computationally expensive task because
theories generally have a number of parameters whose values are not
known a priori. Therefore we have to test a large number of variations
on the theory, generating predictions for many different values of each
parameter in order to identify which regions in parameter space are
ruled out and which are still compatible with existing data.
Contur is a Python toolkit that implements this process, systematically
testing new physics models for consistency with data from the CERN Large
Hadron Collider, so that models can be ruled out quickly where they

conflict with existing results. Contur creates "grids" of results
representing the level of discrepancy between a model and the LHC data
for different values of the model parameters. It does this by comparing
the data with the predictions of the model being tested, and with the
predictions of the Standard Model.
The aim of this project is to investigate how machine learning (ML)
techniques can enhance and extend this process. For example, active
learning [Rocamonde et al] can be used instead of simple parameter
scanning to focus limited computational resources on regions with the
greatest uncertainty in order to map efficiently the regions that are
compatible with existing data. Other possibilties include finding
parameter values that give the best fit between a given effective theory
and LHC data, and searching for anomalies in existing measurements.

Title: Transformers for High Energy Physics

Supervisor 1 email address: g.facini@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: TBA

Work Summary:
Transformer-based machine learning models are reshaping high-energy physics, providing powerful new ways
to tackle some of the field’s hardest problems. The UCL ATLAS group has recently deployed a cutting-edge
tool for identifying b-quarks [1] and calibrating the jets Higgs bosons decay to [2]. similar approaches are
opening the door to physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM) [3]. This project will focus on applying
transformer architectures to Higgs boson tagging at the energy frontier, while also addressing the crucial
question of explainability [4] ensuring that these advanced models are not just accurate, but also interpretable
to physicists.

Higgs boson tagging at the energy frontier: The Higgs boson is the only known scalar particle, and its
properties remain central to the LHC programme. Higgs bosons produced with transverse momenta above 1
TeV could reveal signs of BSM physics [3]. The aim of this project is to develop a transformer-based model,
building on the methods in [1,2], to identify Higgs bosons decaying into two b-quarks in this extreme kinematic
regime and calibrate them to the best possible degree. Afterwards, their performance in collision data needs to
be

Explainability of transformer models: While transformer models are highly effective, their “black-box” nature
poses challenges for physics applications. Recent work within ATLAS has begun to address this issue through
explainable AI methods tailored for HEP [4]. A key goal of this project is to adapt and extend these techniques,
providing insight into what the transformer learns and how its decisions map onto physical features. This will
help build trust in the model’s outputs and deepen our understanding of both the physics and the machine
learning.

[1] https://atlas.web.cern.ch/Atlas/GROUPS/PHYSICS/PUBNOTES/ATL-PHYS-PUB-2023-021/
[2] https://atlas.web.cern.ch/Atlas/GROUPS/PHYSICS/PUBNOTES/ATL-PHYS-PUB-2024-015/
[3] https://atlas.web.cern.ch/Atlas/GROUPS/PHYSICS/PAPERS/HIGG-2021-08/
[4] https://atlas.web.cern.ch/Atlas/GROUPS/PHYSICS/PUBNOTES/ATL-PHYS-PUB-2025-029/

Scientific aims:
The central aim of this project is to deploy transformer-based models in real collision data from the ATLAS
experiment. This requires understanding not only their performance on simulated samples, but also how well
they generalise to the complexities of actual data. By benchmarking, validating, and interpreting these models
on ATLAS Run 3 data, the project will provide critical input for searches at the energy frontier and for improving
the reliability of AI-based methods in particle physics.

Overview:
The project will involve hands-on work in Python using ATLAS software frameworks and machine learning
toolkits. Depending on the student’s background and interests, possible directions include:
Accessing and evaluating the outputs of existing transformer models in collision data.
Implementing and testing explainability techniques to understand model behaviour.
(For advanced students) Training and refining transformer-based models for Higgs tagging.

This project will give experience at the interface of AI and experimental physics, equipping you with
transferable skills in deep learning, explainable AI, and large-scale data analysis.

Title: Using Deep Learning to correct parametric images for motion in dynamic PET

Supervisor 1 email address: k.erlandsson@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Programming experience essential, ideally Python or MATLAB. Basic knowledge of CNN architectures for
imaging and training desired but not required. Interest of making meaningful contributions to research.

Work Summary:
In Positron Emission Tomography (PET) a radiotracer is injected and its distribution is measured, allowing to
investigate metabolic processes related to that molecule in vivo. In dynamic PET, several images are acquired
over time, which are then analysed using kinetic modelling to obtain parametric images corresponding to time
behaviour. However, patient motion is often observed or even unavoidable due to the scan duration (~1 hour).
This can have dramatic impact on the parametric images.
The aim of this project is to investigate the use of CNNs to correct the parametric images for motion. This is
somewhat similar to existing work to remove blurring (“blind deconvolution”), but the impact of motion on
parametric images is quite different. This is a novel approach and could lead to publication.

devices. This project intends to use machine learning techniques to help accomplish this.

name: Franca Fraternali
project_text:
Title: Transformer guided in-silico evolution of Proteins

Supervisor 1 email address: f.fraternali@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: TBA

Supervisor 2 email address: TBA

Pre-Requisites:
Interested students should have strong Python programming skills and some knowledge of Machine Learning.

Overview:
Protein models based on Transformer architecture are advanced computational tools utilized in bioinformatics
and protein engineering. These models operate as neural networks that were trained using vast amounts of
protein sequence data to learn generalized evolutionary constraints. By leveraging their multiple layers of
neurons and attention mechanisms, transformer-based models can be used to predict a plethora of properties
with unprecedented accuracy. Additionally, these structures can also be used for generating new sequences
Insilco that fit desired folds or properties.
Due to their relatively low cost to run, these models expedite the protein design process by generating
extensive libraries of candidate sequences, which can then be experimentally validated for their intended
applications.
The field of Transformer-based models is in continuous evolution, with ongoing advancements in model
architectures and training methodologies. However, challenges such as data bias and model interpretability
must be addressed to ensure the responsible and effective utilization of these powerful computational tools in
protein engineering.
We hypothesise that these models may have biases towards certain patterns that are likely to be
overrepresented on the training data affecting in this way the quality of the predictions.
Techniques: The student will perform an in-silico sequence evolution using state of the art Transformer on a
broad set of proteins spanning different families, stabilities and domains. The project will involve light coding to
run these models and explore the generated sequences. After evolving the sequences, the student will use
other computational libraries (i.e scipy, numpy, matplotlib) to analyse and visualize the changes in the internal
representation of the models (embeddings) to spot undesired trends. Finally, the student will analyse the
presence of those trends in the training data to spot possible sources of the found biases.
Relevant papers:
Lin, Zeming, et al. "Evolutionary-scale prediction of atomic-level protein structure with a language model."
Science 379.6637 (2023): 1123-1130.

Hsu, Chloe, et al. "Learning inverse folding from millions of predicted structures." International conference on
machine learning. PMLR, (2022).
Johnson, Sean R., et al. "Generating novel protein sequences using Gibbs sampling of masked language
models." bioRxiv (2021): 2021-01.
Johnson, Sean R., et al. "Computational scoring and experimental evaluation of enzymes generated by neural
networks." Nature Biotechnology (2024): 1-10.
Meier, Joshua, et al. "Language models enable zero-shot prediction of the effects of mutations on protein
function." Advances in neural information processing systems 34 (2021): 29287-29303.

-----
Title: Hit-to-lead drug discovery via Free Energy calculations and ML

Supervisor 1 email address: f.fraternali@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: TBA

Supervisor 2 email address: TBA

Overview:
Hit-to-lead (H2L) discovery is a key phase in drug development, where initial "hit" compounds from screening
are refined into optimized "lead" candidates. Accurate predictions are crucial in this process. Molecular
dynamics (MD)-based free energy methods, like Free Energy Perturbation (FEP), offer high accuracy but are
slower compared to docking approaches. Recent advancements have improved the performance of MD,
allowing the study of multiple compounds in a single simulation. However, due to the vast chemical space,

manual selection of compounds is still needed. On the other hand, Machine learning (ML) excels at identifying
patterns in compounds quickly but lacks the predictive accuracy of molecular methods. This project aims to
integrate MD and ML to optimise chemical structures by efficiently estimating compound affinity. As MD
simulations progress and more data is gathered, the ML algorithm will suggest compounds that resemble high-
performing binders while avoiding non-binders.
The hypothesis is that combining molecular modelling with ML can improve screening efficiency over
traditional methods. The project involves using MD simulations and ML-based compound selection to estimate
binding free energies, with some coding required for simulation management and result analysis.

Techniques: The student will perform Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations and biding free energies
estimation of compounds of interest selected by ML methods based on embedding similarity. The project will
involve light coding to run the simulations, selected models and to analyze the results.
Relevant papers:
van Gunsteren, Wilfred F., and Chris Oostenbrink. "Methods for Classical-Mechanical Molecular Simulation in
Chemistry: Achievements, Limitations, Perspectives." Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling (2024).
Gracia Carmona, Oriol, and Chris Oostenbrink. "Accelerated enveloping distribution sampling (AEDS) allows for
efficient sampling of orthogonal degrees of freedom." Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling 63.1
(2022): 197-207.
Gim, Mogan, et al. "MolPLA: a molecular pretraining framework for learning cores, R-groups and their linker
joints." Bioinformatics 40. (2024): i369-i380.

name: Jamie Dean
project_text:
Title: Machine Learning for Radiotherapy

Supervisor 1 email address: jamie.dean@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Toby Dixon

Supervisor 2 email address: toby.dixon.23@ucl.ac.uk

Overview:
Paediatric central nervous system tumours are the second most common childhood malignancy. They are
frequently treated with radiotherapy and some of these cancers have relatively high survival rates. However,
patients are often left with debilitating neurocognitive side effects resulting from radiation-induced brain
damage. The developing brain is particularly sensitive to radiation, with different regions expected to be more
or less sensitive at different stages of development. Technological advances in the spatial targeting of
radiotherapy (such as the new UCLH Proton Beam Therapy Centre: https://www.youtube.com/watch?
v=PD0100l65Qc) provide an opportunity to spare the most radiation sensitive regions of the brain to reduce
side effects. However, we do not have a good understanding of which brain regions are most sensitive to
radiotherapy, hampering our ability to exploit these technological advances.

Towards filling this knowledge gap and designing less toxic radiotherapy approaches, we are working on
understanding differences in the radiotherapy response of different brain regions in mice. Specifically, we are
analysing a dataset of mice treated with proton beam radiotherapy, consisting of spatial maps of radiotherapy
dose, digital histology images (cellular resolution microscopy images with different cell types labelled with
markers) and molecular sequencing data quantifying the gene activity of different cell types in different brain
regions.

For this project, you will contribute to our analyses by:
Performing multimodal data integration, mapping the radiotherapy dose maps, digital histology images and
molecular sequencing data onto the same spatial coordinate system with different brain regions defined by a
brain atlas.
Segmenting cells and labelling their identities using state-of-the-art machine learning models.
Measuring differences in abundances and shapes (shape can relate to the activity of cells) of different cell
types in different brain regions in response to radiotherapy.
Performing statistical analyses to identify molecular differences underlying the differential cellular responses to
radiotherapy of different brain regions.

These analyses will reveal the radiation sensitivity of different cell types in different brain regions and the
molecular mechanisms underlying these cellular differences.

Through completing this research, you will gain experience in the application of data integration, state-of-the-
art machine learning and statistical analysis methods while addressing a high priority biomedical problem. No
prior knowledge of biology or medicine is necessary.

name: Adam Gibson
project_text:
Title: Collating variants in early modern printed books

Supervisor 1 email address: adam.gibson@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Prof. Tim Scanlon

Supervisor 2 email address: timothy.scanlon@ucl.ac.uk

Work Summary:
Scholars study early modern printed books by collating multiple surviving copies of a single edition and
identifying differences between the texts. These differences often arise from “stop-press corrections,” where
errors were corrected mid-print-run, resulting in mixed states across copies. Traditionally, collation is done
manually, which is slow, error-prone, and limited by human perception.
This project aims to develop a data-driven, AI-assisted system to automate the collation process. You will
work with a large dataset of digitized pages from early modern books. The goal is to identify subtle variations
in the texts between digitised images of pages using image processing and machine learning techniques.
Challenges include:
Handling page curvature, warping, and bleed-through
Aligning images taken under different digitisation systems
Distinguishing printed text from annotations and artefacts
Exploring alternatives to OCR, such as pixel-based comparison on a coordinate grid
You will develop algorithms for preprocessing the digitised images, registration, detecting variants, and
classifying the variants into types. It will also be important to think about the user interface, and how you can
display your results to a scholar. The project may involve supervised learning using labelled examples, or
unsupervised clustering of page states. A successful proof-of-concept could significantly improve the speed
and accuracy of textual collation in digital humanities.
This open-ended project will suit student with an interest in problem-solving and applying AI to historical or
cultural data. Supervisors: Adam Gibson, Tim Scanlon and Chris Stamtakis

name: Jon Butterworth
project_text:
Title: Optimising the Contur toolkit for testing new theories in particle physics

Supervisor 1 email address: J.Butterworth@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Dr. Ben Waugh

Supervisor 2 email address: B.Waugh@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Familiarity with some (but not necessarily all, as you can learn some during the project) of the following:
UNIX shell, python, SQL and database technologies, git.

Work Summary:
A major area of research in particle physics is testing new BSM (Beyond
the Standard Model) theories by comparing their predictions with known
experimental results. This is a computationally expensive task because
theories generally have a number of parameters whose values are not
known a priori. Therefore we have to test a large number of variations
on the theory, generating predictions for many different values of each
parameter in order to identify which regions in parameter space are
ruled out and which are still compatible with existing data.
Contur is a Python toolkit that implements this process, systematically
testing new physics models for consistency with data from the CERN Large
Hadron Collider, so that models can be ruled out quickly where they
conflict with existing results. Contur creates "grids" of results
representing the level of discrepancy between a model and the LHC data
for different values of the model parameters. It does this by comparing
the data with the predictions of the model being tested, and with the
predictions of the Standard Model.
The predictions are expressed as a set of histograms for each point in
the grid. From previous projects, a database design has been created and
implemented, in which the relational information between models, grids,
parameters, exclusions and histograms can be stored. A basic interactive
interface has also been developed. However, given the large numbers of
results that need to be handled when varying multiple parameters,
analysis using Contur is time consuming and requires significant
computational resources.

The aim of this project is to optimise the code and the database so that
results can be obtained more quickly and explored more effectively. This
might involve benchmarking and profiling the Python code, analysing
database queries, and implementing and testing techniques to improve the
performance of Contur.

name: Maxim Molodsov
project_text:
Title: How do cells compact and reorganize DNA?

Supervisor 1 email address: maxim.molodtsov@crick.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: TBA

Supervisor 2 email address: TBA

Work Summary:
DNA is a very long linear molecule that encodes genetic information in a sequence of chemicals frequently
denoted as A, T, G and C. Each cell in the human body contains one complete set of the whole body’s genome
and therefore DNA needs to be extremely compact inside each cell. If all DNA just from one single cell could be
stretched into a line, it would be almost 2 meters long (and 2 nanometres thick)!
How cells achieve this extreme compaction and yet keep the ability to have access to the genetic information,
read, copy and repair genes is still poorly understood.
Recently two distinct mechanisms have been identified that play crucial roles in the DNA organization. One is
based on multiple weak multivalent interactions between nucleosomes – tiny building blocks of the genome –
that due to multiple attractive interactions form liquid-like condensates. The second mechanism called loop
extrusion uses unusual activity of a molecular machine called condensin, which can actively move along DNA
and make DNA loops. However, how these mechanisms work together is still largely unknown.
This project will use LAMMPS molecular dynamics simulator (www.lammps.org) to test how these molecular
mechanisms integrate mechanistically. It is aimed for a student with a strong interest in biology and good
modelling experience.

Title: Clock-Rates on the Surface of the Moon

Supervisor 1 email address: ucapael@ucl.ac.uk

Overview:
A result of General Relativity is that clock-rates depend on the gravitational field in which
the clock is located. In particular, a clock near the Moon's selenoid ticks faster than one
near the Earth's geoid by roughly 56 microseconds per day. Astronomical observations made on
the lunar surface, timed with clocks on the Moon's surface, need those times to be corrected to
the time that would have been recorded had those observations been made at the Solar System
Barycentre. The project objective is to write a computer program to make the time correction
that would be required.

The ExoMol project is the world’s leading provider of high-temperature molecular data for modelling exoplanet

name: Federico Galvanin
project_text:
Title: Application of model-based design of experiments to develop a digital twin for liquid-liquid extraction systems for precious metals recovery

Supervisor 1 email address: f.galvanin@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Dr. Arun Pankajakshan

Supervisor 2 email address: arun.pankajakshan.16@ucl.ac.uk

Pre-Requisites:
Digital technologies are at the forefront of accelerated chemical process development. The core of such
technologies is a digital twin, which in simple terms is a mathematical model of the physical system, which
continuously interacts with the system and makes best decisions to meet specified goals related to product
and process quality. In this project, we will be applying model-based design of experiments (MBDoE) methods
[1] to develop a digital twin for the recovery of precious metals in continuous flow small channels using liquid-
liquid extraction (LLE). LLE in small channels often leads to segmented flow in which two immiscible liquids
move in a repeating pattern of slugs and plugs [2]. The geometry of this flow pattern and the derived

hydrodynamic properties based on it determine the rate of mass transfer between the liquid phases. A
mathematical model for the segmented flow thus involves modelling hydrodynamics followed by mass transfer.
While data-driven modelling approaches are commonly used to model hydrodynamics, the mass transfer
model can be developed using first principles. As a result, we propose a joint system identification framework
that leverages MBDoE methods and its machine learning counterpart – active learning [3], for the joint
identification of the data-driven and physics-based parts of a hybrid segmented flow model, thereby
developing the digital twin for the LLE system. The identified digital twin model will then be used for LLE
process simulation and for scenario-based optimization.
The student will be jointly supervised by Prof. Federico Galvanin, Prof. Panagiota Angeli and Dr. Arun
Pankajakshan.
References
[1] G. Franceschini and S. Macchietto, “Model-based design of experiments for parameter precision: State
of the art,” Chem Eng Sci, vol. 63, no. 19, 2008, doi: 10.1016/j.ces.2007.11.034.
[2] E. Garciadiego-Ortega, D. Tsaoulidis, M. Pineda, E. S. Fraga, and P. Angeli, “Hydrodynamics and mass
transfer in segmented flow small channel contactors for uranium extraction,” Chemical Engineering and
Processing - Process Intensification, vol. 153, 2020, doi: 10.1016/j.cep.2020.107921.
[3] D. D. Lewis and J. Catlett, “Heterogeneous Uncertainty Sampling for Supervised Learning,” in
Proceedings of the 11th International Conference on Machine Learning, ICML 1994, 1994. doi: 10.1016/B978-1-
55860-335-6.50026-X.

name: Siyin Liu
project_text:
Title: AI-Powered Discovery of Digital Biomarkers in Common Corneal Disease

Supervisor 1 email address: siyin.liu@ucl.ac.uk

Supervisor 2 name: Will Woof

Supervisor 2 email address: w.woof@ucl.ac.uk

Overview:
A Brief Introduction/Background
Corneal diseases are a major cause of blindness worldwide, and many patients ultimately require corneal
transplantation. At Moorfields Eye Hospital, advanced imaging plays a vital role in diagnosis and monitoring.
One of the most powerful tools is In-Vivo Confocal Microscopy (IVCM), which provides real-time, cellular-level
views of the living human cornea.
IVCM produces high-resolution, information-rich datasets that can reveal how corneal diseases progress over
time. However, the sheer volume and complexity of these images make manual analysis time-consuming,
subjective, and a bottleneck for both clinical care and research.
This MSc project will focus on using Fuchs Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy (FECD) as the primary disease
model. FECD is a common, sight-threatening genetic disorder affecting up to 5% of people over 40 and is the
leading reason for corneal transplantation in high-income countries . A hallmark of FECD is its long, silent
preclinical phase, in which subtle cellular changes occur decades before symptoms arise. This period
represents a critical opportunity for intervention with future gene-based therapies.
A key barrier to such treatments is the lack of sensitive, quantitative imaging endpoints suitable for clinical
trials in early disease. This project aims to address this gap by developing and validating a state-of-the-art
deep learning pipeline for automated, quantitative IVCM image analysis, enabling the discovery of novel,
unbiased digital biomarkers of FECD progression .

Methodology
This project will leverage a unique dataset of IVCM images from the FECD-TRACE cohort, a longitudinal study
that is one of the first to include the full spectrum of disease, from preclinical genetic carriers to late-stage
patients.
The core task will be to design, train, and validate an end-to-end deep learning pipeline for the automated
analysis of these images. While the project's specific focus can be tailored to the student's interests, it will
involve tackling key computer vision challenges. This could range from developing robust classifiers for image
quality control, to building sophisticated segmentation models for the quantification of cellular pathology, or to
explore self-supervised learning with Vision Transformers (e.g., DINO) to perform representation learning and
discover novel, unbiased 'digital biomarkers', with the potential to link these features to our curated clinical and
genetic data. The student will be responsible for data pre-processing, model training and tuning, and rigorous
validation of their results.

References
1. Liu S, Sadan AN, Bhattacharyya N, et al. Genetic and demographic determinants of Fuchs endothelial
